extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and students/scholars of poetics and dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetic and dramatic works (particularly tragedy and epic): medium, plot, character, diction, spectacle, and practical rules for the tragic poet. Classical/theoretical guidance useful to creative writers and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (μίμησις) as the governing principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and allied arts are fundamentally modes of imitation (μίμησις); the imitation is the common principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation should be understood with respect to three distinguishing factors — the medium (the material vehicle), the objects imitated, and the manner of imitation — each of which helps define genre and method (e.g., tragedy vs comedy vs epic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation: rhythm, language, harmony (melody)
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium or material vehicle of poetic imitation is rhythm, language, and 'harmony' (or melody), taken singly or in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and exploit the appropriate medium for the effect sought: some arts use harmony and rhythm (music, lyre), some rhythm alone (dance), some language alone (narrative in prose or verse), and some combine them (tragedy, dithyrambs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: represent higher/lower/actual types
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are men in action, who must be represented as better than in life, worse than in life, or as they are; this distinction is the basis for differentiating genres (e.g., tragedy vs comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to idealize (make characters nobler), to represent them as typical/true-to-life, or to depict them as worse; each choice has implications for tone and moral effect (Polygnotus vs Pauson vs Dionysius examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: drama vs narrative vs mixed forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may take the form of dramatic presentation, pure narrative (including lyric), or pure drama; the manner of imitation distinguishes subgenres and affects technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious whether you are showing action (dramatic) or telling it (narrative) and use the conventions appropriate to each; mixed/combined manners require careful handling of medium and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent elements of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has six elements: three 'external' — Scenic Presentment (spectacle, ὄψις), Lyrical Song (μελοποιία), Diction (λέξις); and three 'internal' — Plot (μῦθος), Character (ἤθος), and Thought (διάνοια).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot (mythos) is of primary importance; character and thought follow in importance. Spectacle is least intrinsic to poetic art (belongs more to performance) though it affects vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (μῦθος)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot — the representation of action — is of primary importance in tragedy; the arrangement and sequence of incidents chiefly determine the tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the plot first: its wholeness, unity, magnitude, and causal sequence determine the work's power to produce pity and fear. Character and thought should serve the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole: completeness and adequate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot should contain all necessary parts to produce the intended effect without extraneous material; its size must suit the unity aimed for (too long dilutes effect; too short may seem truncated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists not in unity of hero but in unity of action: the parts must be organically connected into a single, coherent action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unrelated subplots that do not contribute to the principal action; every incident should follow by probable or necessary sequence to preserve unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic (universal) truth versus historical (particular) truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic unity and acceptability rest on poetic truth — the expression of the universal — not on strict historical particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate incidents by whether they exemplify what generally happens (probable) or must happen (necessary) in the way poetry requires, rather than by literal factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence for incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents in a plot should be ordered by probable or necessary sequence so that the action seems coherent and inevitable within the poem's logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arranging events, ensure each follows from preceding circumstances plausibly; sequences that violate probability or necessity risk breaking unity and audience belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best tragic effects: combination of the inevitable and the unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The most powerful tragic effects arise from a combination of the inevitable and the unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct reversals and recognitions so that the outcome feels both surprising and, on reflection, unavoidable; balance surprise with logical necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple (ἁπλοῖ) and Complex (πεπλεγμένοι) plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple plots involve change without reversal/recognition; complex plots include reversal (περιπέτεια), recognition (ἀναγνώρισις), and pathos (πάθος).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complex structure (reversal + recognition) when aiming for deeper tragic impact; recognize the different emotional and structural demands of simple versus complex forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal) as a structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia — a sudden reversal of the action — is a key moment that changes the hero's situation toward good or ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place reversals so they arise from the plot's internal logic; the reversal should be both surprising and necessary, enhancing the tragic effect rather than feeling contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (recognition) and its varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is the discovery by a character of a key fact (identity, relationship, cause) and comes in various kinds; it often operates with peripeteia to produce pathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ recognitions that are organically prepared by the plot's clues and that transform the hero's understanding in a way that is emotionally and logically satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (πάθος) — tragic incident that arouses pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathos denotes a tragic or disastrous incident; it is an essential element that arouses pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pathos grows from the plot's internal necessities (not from spectacle) so that pity and fear are properly grounded in the action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divisible into quantitative parts (μέρη κατὰ τὸ ποσόν) such as prologue, episodes, choral odes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these parts to structure the progression of the action; however, be mindful some sections of the ancient text may be interpolated — treat formal divisions as tools, not rigid prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic action requirements: change of fortune and hero's character
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes tragic action includes a change of fortune and the character of the hero: the hero must be such that the reversal is credible and fitting to character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or craft heroes whose moral purpose and disposition make their fall (or change) probable; the most tragic endings (unhappy) often better realize tragedy's aims than 'poetic justice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and fear must spring from the Plot itself (avoid dependence on spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring from the plot itself; to produce them by scenery or spectacular effect is contrary to the spirit of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plot-based elicitation of emotion; spectacle may enhance vividness but is a lower element and should not substitute for structural causes of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ἤθος) as manifestation of moral purpose and subject to probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is the manifestation of moral purpose; ethical portraiture must observe necessity or probability as in plot — characters' actions must be believable in light of their disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid caricature or inconsistent traits; idealize or adjust character only insofar as it serves the plot's plausibility and the poem's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina and out-of-place resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolutions that are out of place (e.g., deus ex machina) are criticized as improper; the ending should arise from the plot's internal causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce arbitrary external contrivances to solve complications; denouement should be the natural result of earlier incidents and recognition/reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule: place the scene before the poet and act the parts
rubrics_metrics.description: One practical rule for the tragic poet is to place the scene before his eyes and to act the parts himself in order to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visualization and embodiment (imaginative acting) during composition to ensure characters and actions are lived and convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule: sketch the bare outline (skeleton) before filling episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch the bare outline of the action (the skeleton) before proceeding to fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the essential structure and key turning points first; then compose episodes and speeches that serve that structure rather than allowing episodes to dictate the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of complication (δῆλος/δέος) and denouement (λύσις)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must be careful about the complication and the denouement of the plot, especially ensuring a proper dénouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange complications so they lead logically to the dénouement; the resolution should fulfill the plot's promises and produce catharsis without contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine varied poetic excellences but avoid overloading with epic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, unite varied forms of poetic excellence; but do not overcharge a tragedy with details appropriate to epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance inclusion of elevated techniques (lyric, metaphor) with the unity and concision required by tragedy; avoid epic-length scope and superfluous narrative detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choral odes and songs must be organic to the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Choral odes—like the dialogue—should be an organic part of the whole and integrated with the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral passages to advance or comment on action in ways that reinforce unity and emotional effect, not as digressive ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (διάνοια) as the intellectual element expressed by speeches or incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought denotes the intellectual element, which may be expressed either by rhetorical speeches or through dramatic incidents that speak for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the reasoning and ideas in the play are embodied in action as well as in rhetoric; thought should arise naturally from character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (λέξις) and poetic diction: elevation with perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction pertains to language and modes of speech; poetic diction includes permissible words and figures (notably metaphor). Poetry should combine elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elevated language and metaphor where appropriate, but preserve clarity; diction often overlaps with declamatory art, so match style to medium and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: unity of action, length, metre, and the art of plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic agrees with tragedy in unity of action but differs in length, metre, and the techniques of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction; tragedy achieves a concentrated, vivid pleasure and completes its effect within narrower limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing mode, prefer tragedy for tightly unified, concentrated treatment of a single action; use epic when scope and multiplicity of episodes are required, but be mindful of dilution of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling critical objections: five common charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics censure works as impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, contradictory, or artistically incorrect; answers should be sought under twelve heads (artistic reasons, necessity, probability, received opinion, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to objections by showing how artistic requirements, poetic truth, or accepted belief justify a poet's choices; analyze claims for equivocation, and appeal to internal coherence and necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for 'probable impossibility' over 'improbable possibility'
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to artistic requirements, a probable impossibility (the idealized or higher thing that transcends reality) may be preferable to a merely improbable but possible event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists may legitimately present idealized or 'impossible' beings if such presentations serve the poetic purpose and elevate the example; justify departures from strict realism by appeal to the work's aim and universals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful interpretation of language and multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word or phrase seems inconsistent, consider how many senses it may bear in the passage; avoid jumping to groundless conclusions based on a single, literal reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets alike should examine semantic range and context, and prefer readings that preserve poetic coherence and internal justification rather than forcing perceived contradictions.
